text: This is the final lesson of the entire Cloud Engineer to Cloud Architect path. It closes fifteen courses, and it deserves a real look back rather than a quick wrap-up -- tracing this chapter's four lessons, this course's eight chapters, and the whole three-stage arc that led here.

This chapter's labs and case study used every earlier chapter of this course. Chapter 1's error budgets are why the tiered RTO and RPO targets read as business tradeoffs, not arbitrary numbers. Chapter 2's incident command roles became the game day's Incident Commander, Scribe, and Comms lead. Chapter 3 is why the chaos experiment had a hypothesis and abort criteria instead of just breaking something to see. Chapter 4's dependency mapping is the backbone of the DR plan, and the reason the case study's single point of failure existed to be found at all. Chapters 5 through 7 shaped the measured failover target, the automated runbook, and the blameless debrief that followed.

This course is one of four Expert Specialization courses, alongside Advanced Platform Engineering and GitOps, Hybrid and Multi-Cloud Enterprise Architecture, and AI Cloud Infrastructure and MLOps. The path's own outline says these four build on the Advanced stage but not on each other, so they can be taken in any order once complete. SRE is a different lens on the same infrastructure the other three build, not a sequel to any one of them.

The full path is three stages and fifteen courses. Job-Ready Foundation's seven courses took a Cloud Support Engineer from not knowing what a subnet was through a real deployment capstone. Advanced Specialization's four courses turned that engineer into an architect through infrastructure as code, containers, reliability and FinOps, and an enterprise capstone. Expert Specialization's four parallel courses, this one included, are doors out of that same Cloud Architect floor.

This path's own destination note states the arc directly: Cloud Support or Junior Cloud Engineer, to Cloud Engineer, to Cloud Architect, with Expert Specialization opening doors toward Platform Engineer, Multi-Cloud or Enterprise Architect, AI Infrastructure Engineer, or Site Reliability Engineer roles. Not a promised title at graduation -- the realistic shape of the climb, and this course is the SRE door at the top of it.

Fifteen courses, one argument: design a disaster recovery plan, automate its failover, prove it under real chaos and a rehearsed team response, and keep asking what's still quietly depending on a single point of failure. That question, asked again and again, is the whole arc this path was built to deliver.
